newsitem.title: USA: NASA adds fifth spacewalk to patch-up Hubble.
newsitem.headline: NASA adds fifth spacewalk to patch-up Hubble.

text.p: Shuttle astronauts were told on Sunday to take an extra spacewalk to patch up the Hubble Space Telescope's torn and tattered exterior.

Repairs were ordered because scientists feared that rips in the silvery foil, which insulates the telescope's interior from the harsh environment of space, could cause crucial electronics to overheat and fail.
Flight controllers instructed the astronauts to start the repair effort on Sunday night's planned outing into space and finish the work during an extra spacewalk scheduled for Monday.
"A fifth EVA (spacewalk) has been approved," mission control's Kay Hire informed the seven-man crew.

After completing the two remaining servicing tasks on Sunday, the astronauts were to patch up two long rips in the insulation near the top of the four-story telescope. Then, on Monday night, during a three- or four-hour excursion, they would tackle three compartments containing electronics.
"We have an opportunity to put a couple of Band-Aids on and we are going to go do that," said Mike Weiss, a Hubble systems manager.

The makeshift patches will be lashed to the side of the telescope using wire and rope. The astronauts will have to fashion some of the blankets from narrow strips of insulation, using a repair kit improvised from adhesive tape, ropes, electrical wire and metal clips.

Jerry Ross, a veteran of four spacewalks, and Jeff Hoffman, who flew on the last Hubble repair mission, were to test the procedure on a mock-up of the telescope in a water tank near the Johnson Space Centre.
Hubble project officials said they were confident they could find ways of keeping the telescope cool if necessary, but were making the repairs as a precautionary measure.
"We've got a $2 billion investment here. Why take a chance?" Ed Weiler, Hubble's chief astronomer, said.

Astronauts Greg Harbaugh and Joe Tanner began the fourth spacewalk of the mission at about 10:50 p.m. EST on Sunday (0350 GMT on Monday). They were to replace an electronics box that controls the telescope's solar panels and replace covers on magnetic sensors before starting work on the telescope's battered exterior.
Earlier on Sunday, astronauts Mark Lee and Steve Smith, on the mission's third spacewalk, took a closeup look at some of the damage.

"Basically this thing is just falling apart, cracking all over the place," Lee told mission control as he inspected a foil-covered door on the telescope. He tried taping up a crack but as NASA engineers had feared the adhesive failed to hold.
"It barely sticks," he said. "It doesn't do anything."
Lee and Smith collected pieces of spare foil, tape and cords aboard the shuttle for the possible repair attempt.

Engineers suspected variations in temperature and ultraviolet rays from the sun had caused the silvery foil to crack and tear. The damage, which appeared extensive, was not seen when astronauts last visited the telescope in 1993.

Lee and Smith upgraded three more components of the telescope during their seven-hour spacewalk. They completed what was considered the most challenging task of the effort, the replacement of a faulty electronics box.

The swap-out of the data interface unit, which relays computer commands to various telescope components, was difficult because the device was not designed to be handled by astronauts wearing bulky space suit gloves.
Working in a jumble of wires, Lee had to make 18 cable connections to complete the installation. "Great hands, Mark," mission control's Hoffman radioed once the work was done.
The two men then went on to exchange an ageing reel-to-reel tape recorder for a new digital model and replace a broken flywheel device used to manoeuvre the telescope.
Between tasks, the astronauts marvelled at the spectacular view as the shuttle soared more than 370 miles (595 km) above the Pacific, off the west coast of Australia.
"Holy cow!" Lee exclaimed. "I've got the Hubble Space Telescope, Shark's Bay, and the planet Earth and the moon in my view. What a great place to be."
"Just an average day for a couple of spacewalkers," Joe Tanner remarked from inside the shuttle's cabin.

As the astronauts ended their spacewalk, shuttle commander Ken Bowersox and copilot Scott Horowitz fired the smallest manoeuvring jets aboard for 20 minutes to nudge Hubble into a higher orbit. NASA hopes to boost the telescope's altitude by a total of six or seven miles to prolong its life.
